title: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
hook: Kabir (the dohas, one a day for a week)
carry: the musk is in the deer
tomorrow: Tulsidas (the Ramcharitmanas opening and the Hanuman Chalisa, verse by verse)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kabir's second doha: reading book after book, no one became wise, but whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit. Whose love did you read today? Day nine hundred twenty-three.

A deer is moving through the forest, head low, nose working. There's a scent in the air, rich and sweet, and it's maddening, because it's everywhere and nowhere. The deer checks behind a tree. Under a bush. Down by the stream. The scent is just as strong in each place, and never any closer. It keeps searching until it's worn out. Kabir put this deer in two lines. It's our third doha, and our last day with the weaver of Kashi.
screen: `A SCENT IN THE FOREST.` → `EVERYWHERE AND NOWHERE.` → `THE DEER KEEPS SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: The doha begins, in Hindi, kasturi kundal basai. Kasturi is musk, the prized scent. In English, roughly: the musk lives in the deer's own navel, and the deer goes searching for it through the forest. Then the second line: just so, Ram is in every body, every heart, and the world doesn't see. The joke is gentle, and the deer stands for anyone who searches. The scent was never out there. It was coming from the one doing the searching. Every place smelled of musk because the deer brought it to every place. Notice what Ram means in Kabir's mouth. It's the name his teacher cried out on the steps at Kashi. But Kabir's Ram isn't held in one temple or one image. In this doha, Ram is in every heart, and the trouble is only that we look everywhere else first. So put the three dohas together. Day one: go looking for the bad one, and you end up searching your own heart. Day two: read book after book, and still the lesson is two and a half letters, love. Day three: search the whole forest for God, and the scent was in you all along. Three hunts, and each one turns back toward the hunter. Kabir's life ends, tradition says, with one more turn. When he died, two groups of his followers, Hindus and Muslims, each wanted to give him their own last rites. Some say they argued over the body. When they lifted the sheet, there was no body there at all, only a heap of flowers. So each group took half the flowers, and honored him in its own way.
screen: `THE MUSK IS IN THE DEER.` · `RAM IN EVERY HEART.` · `THREE HUNTS, TURNED BACK.` · then, large: `ONLY FLOWERS UNDER THE SHEET.`

segments.voice: Sit still, and let the searching part of you rest. Notice the breath coming in and going out, without going anywhere to get it. It's already here. If your mind runs off into the forest, after a plan, a worry, a thing you want, that's fine; notice it, the way you'd notice the deer, and come back to the breath. Nothing to find. Just staying with what's already here, the way the musk was already in the deer. If you pray, you can rest in God as near as your own breath. The bell holds the time.
Kabir. The weaver-poet of Kashi. Today's doha: the musk is in the deer's own navel, and it searches the forest; Ram is in every heart, and the world doesn't see.
Your line: the musk is in the deer. Today, when you catch yourself hunting for something outside, check first whether the scent is coming from you. Day nine hundred twenty-three.

screen: `DAY 923 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TULSIDAS (THE RAMCHARITMANAS OPENING AND THE HANUMAN CHALISA, VERSE BY VERSE).`

howItsDone: The musk deer doha is quoted as a saying about looking for God far away, and the story of the flowers under Kabir's sheet is told by people of more than one community who honor him.

match.prompt: Kabir's three dohas — tap the pairs.
pairs: reads two and a half letters

myth: in the doha, the deer finds the musk behind a tree
it searches the forest, but the musk is in its own navel.
Kabir's Ram, in this doha, is in every heart
the world doesn't see, the second line says.
tradition says Kabir's followers found his body and buried it
under the sheet they found only flowers, and each group took half.

fork.setup: you're the deer in Kabir's doha. a sweet scent is everywhere, and never any closer. what does the doha say you do?
options: search the whole forest for it.
follow the stream out of the forest.
fork.reveal: the deer searches the forest, but the musk is in its own navel. Kabir says Ram is in every heart, and the world doesn't see.

original.note: Hindi, in Devanagari: musk, the scent the deer searches for in today's doha.

trapdoor: what you thought: a nature poem about a deer.
what it means: the thing we hunt for everywhere was in the hunter all along; Ram is in every heart.
what a scholar hears: ghat ghat in the second line is pot after pot, the body pictured as a clay vessel, so Ram lives in every one.

notes: The doha is paraphrased, with only its opening words in Hindi transliteration, unquoted. Confirm wording, especially the second line (ghat ghat, 'in every body / every heart').

The death story is framed as tradition; confirm the telling (two communities, the sheet, the flowers divided). It is told as shared ground and does not rank either community; a Keeper should confirm the tone.
Kabir's Ram is described as not held in one temple or image, drawn from this doha; a Keeper may want to say more carefully how Kabir uses the name.
The outline promised a week of dohas; this is the third and last Kabir day. Owner may want to align the title.
Original: कस्तूरी, stress guide kas-TOO-ree; confirm.

Editor pass: fixed 'the name he cried out on the steps' (in day 921 it was Ramananda who cried Ram, Ram, not Kabir); cut the invented 'Kabir watched this deer'; 'the deer is all of us' softened to 'stands for anyone who searches'.
Audit pass: trapdoor third floor replaced (it restated the three-doha summary) with the sense of ghat ghat as pot after pot, the body as a vessel; confirm the gloss.
